facts.text: In 1947 Harvard Mark II operators taped a moth into their logbook: "First actual case of bug being found." Engineers already said bug long before.
ENIAC, finished in 1945, weighed about 27 tonnes and took up some 167 square metres of floor.
Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email in 1971 and picked the @ sign to separate the user from the host.
The Apollo Guidance Computer had 2,048 words of erasable memory, about 4 KB, and 36,864 words of rope memory woven by hand.
IBM's first hard disk drive, the 350 of 1956, held about 3.75 MB on fifty 24-inch platters.
The Antikythera mechanism, built over 2,000 years ago, used bronze gears to predict astronomical events.
Ada Lovelace's 1843 notes included an algorithm intended for Charles Babbage's unbuilt Analytical Engine.
Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine with separate processing and memory units in the 1830s.
The Jacquard loom used punched cards to control woven patterns long before computers used them for data.
Herman Hollerith's punched-card machines helped process the 1890 US census.
Konrad Zuse completed the Z3 in 1941, an early working programmable electromechanical computer.
The Colossus computers at Bletchley Park helped British codebreakers analyze encrypted wartime messages.
The Manchester Baby ran its first stored program on 21 June 1948.
The Ferranti Mark 1, delivered in 1951, was among the earliest commercially available general-purpose computers.
Grace Hopper popularized the idea of machine-independent programming languages and worked on early compilers.
UNIVAC I famously helped predict the 1952 US presidential election result on television.
The first computer mouse prototype, demonstrated by Douglas Engelbart, had a wooden shell.
Engelbart's 1968 'Mother of All Demos' showed a mouse, hypertext, video conferencing and collaborative editing.
Core memory stored bits using tiny magnetic rings threaded by wires.
The first Intel 4004 microprocessor, released in 1971, had roughly 2,300 transistors.
The Altair 8800 inspired the creation of Microsoft after appearing on a magazine cover in 1975.
The Apple I was sold as a circuit board, not a finished computer with a case and keyboard.
The IBM PC launched in 1981 with an Intel 8088 processor.
The original Macintosh of 1984 had a nine-inch monochrome screen and 128 KB of RAM.
The Xerox Star introduced a desktop-style interface in 1981, but its high price limited sales to roughly 25,000 units.
The Xerox Alto, introduced in 1973, featured a graphical interface and a mouse.
A floppy disk's magnetic surface is flexible even though the 3.5-inch disk has a rigid plastic shell.
The original 8-inch floppy disks were introduced by IBM in the early 1970s.
The Commodore 64 became one of the best-selling single computer models ever made.
The Sinclair ZX81 was sold with just 1 KB of RAM in its base configuration.
IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match in 1997.
The Cray-1 supercomputer had a distinctive C-shaped cabinet that helped shorten wiring distances.
A vacuum tube computer could fail when a single thermionic valve stopped working.
Early computers often used delay lines, literally storing data as traveling pulses of sound.
The Williams tube stored digital data as charged spots on the surface of a cathode-ray tube.
The first commercially available CD-ROM drives appeared in the mid-1980s.
The original IBM PC used cassette tape storage as an option alongside floppy disk drives.
CSIRAC played some of the earliest computer music in Australia in the early 1950s.
The first hard disk drives were so large that moving them often required industrial equipment.
The term 'computer' originally described a person performing calculations, not a machine.
Alan Turing's 1936 paper described an abstract machine that became a foundation of computability theory.
The Harvard Mark I, completed in 1944, used electromechanical relays and mechanical counters.
Punched tape stored instructions or data as patterns of holes in a strip of paper.
Spacewar!, created at MIT in 1962, ran on the PDP-1 and became an influential early computer game.
The PDP-8, released in 1965, helped popularize smaller and more affordable minicomputers.
The first IBM PC keyboard had 83 keys; today's familiar keyboard layouts came later.
In 1973, Xerox PARC's Ethernet prototype connected computers over a shared coaxial cable.
The first SMS text message, 'Merry Christmas', was sent in 1992.
The Osborne 1, sold in 1981, weighed about 11 kilograms despite being marketed as portable.
The first commercial flash memory products appeared decades after the first magnetic core computers.
Python is named after Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake: Guido van Rossum was reading its scripts at the time.
Brendan Eich wrote the first version of JavaScript in about ten days in May 1995, at Netscape.
Java was first called Oak, after an oak tree outside James Gosling's office.
C# was first developed under the name Cool, short for "C-like Object Oriented Language".
FORTRAN's name is short for 'Formula Translation'; its first compiler was released by IBM in 1957.
COBOL was designed in 1959 to make business programs more portable across different computers.
The C language grew out of B at Bell Labs while Unix was being developed.
Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson rewrote much of Unix in C, making it easier to port to new machines.
The name C++ reflects the C increment operator ++, suggesting a step beyond C.
Bjarne Stroustrup initially called C++ 'C with Classes'.
Rust was originally a personal project by Graydon Hoare before Mozilla sponsored it.
Go was designed at Google by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson.
The name 'Perl' was chosen by Larry Wall before the expansion 'Practical Extraction and Report Language'.
Ruby's creator Yukihiro Matsumoto wanted a language that felt enjoyable for programmers.
PHP originally stood for 'Personal Home Page'; its modern recursive name is 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Java bytecode runs on the Java Virtual Machine rather than directly on one specific CPU.
JavaScript and Java are separate languages despite their similar names.
TypeScript extends JavaScript with a type system that is erased when code is compiled.
Python's indentation is part of its syntax, not merely a style convention.
In Python, 'True' and 'False' are instances of bool, which is a subclass of int.
Java's checked exceptions must generally be caught or declared by methods that can throw them.
C# distinguishes value types from reference types, but both ultimately derive from System.Object.
In C#, 'async' methods do not automatically run on a new thread.
The first release of C# and the .NET Framework arrived in 2002.
SQL is a declarative language: you describe the result, and the database chooses how to obtain it.
SQL's NULL follows three-valued logic: a comparison can be unknown, not just true or false.
The first standard version of SQL was published by ANSI in 1986.
Erlang was created at Ericsson for fault-tolerant telecommunications systems.
Elixir runs on the Erlang virtual machine and inherits its process-based concurrency model.
Haskell is named after logician Haskell Curry, not a style of cooking.
Scheme, a Lisp dialect, was created in the 1970s by Guy Steele and Gerald Sussman.
Smalltalk helped popularize object-oriented programming and graphical development environments.
Alan Kay helped develop Smalltalk in the 1970s; its message-passing ideas influenced generations of object-oriented languages.
The original BASIC language was created at Dartmouth College in 1964.
Assembly language represents machine instructions with human-readable mnemonics.
A language can be Turing-complete even if its syntax looks nothing like conventional code.
Brainfuck uses only eight commands but is still Turing-complete in its idealized form.
Whitespace treats spaces, tabs and line breaks as instructions while ignoring most visible characters.
Prolog expresses rules and relationships rather than a sequence of commands.
OCaml combines functional programming with mutable state and object-oriented features.
Kotlin was developed by JetBrains and became a first-class language for Android development.
Swift was introduced by Apple in 2014 as a modern language for its platforms.
The original Lua language was developed in Brazil for scripting and configuration tasks.
R traces its roots to S, a statistical programming language created at Bell Labs.
Julia supports multiple dispatch, choosing methods based on the types of several arguments.
A regex can be useful without being a full parser for every possible programming language.
In JavaScript, typeof null returns 'object', a behavior retained for compatibility.
In JavaScript, NaN is not equal to itself: NaN === NaN evaluates to false.
The Ada language was named in honor of Ada Lovelace and standardized in the 1980s.
The first version of Objective-C added Smalltalk-style messaging to C.
HTTP status 418, "I'm a teapot", comes from a 1998 April Fools' RFC about controlling coffee pots over the internet.
symbolics.com, registered on 15 March 1985, was the first .com domain name.
One of the first webcams watched a coffee pot in Cambridge's Trojan Room, so people could see if it was empty before walking over.
Tim Berners-Lee's first browser, WorldWideWeb (1990), was also an editor: you could write pages, not just read them.
Even if every website vanished, email and many other internet services could still work: the Web is only one layer of the internet.
ARPANET's first message in 1969 was meant to be 'LOGIN' but the system crashed after 'LO'.
The internet's TCP/IP transition on 1 January 1983 is often called its 'flag day'.
The domain name system went live in the 1980s so users could stop memorizing host addresses from a growing central file.
The DNS record that sends your email to a mail server is MX; a domain can handle mail even without hosting a website.
DNS usually starts with UDP, but large replies and some other situations may switch it to TCP.
IPv6 offers 2^128 addresses, about 340 undecillion, compared with IPv4’s roughly 4.3 billion.
The part after # in a typical URL never reaches the server in an HTTP request; the browser interprets it locally.
The first public web search engines appeared years before Google launched in 1998.
Archie, created in 1990, indexed FTP file listings rather than web pages.
The term 'surfing the internet' became popular in the early 1990s.
HTTP requests do not remember earlier requests by themselves, so websites add cookies or tokens to maintain sessions.
HTTPS can encrypt the connection to a phishing site just as effectively as it encrypts a legitimate site.
The fake login site paypal.example can have perfectly valid HTTPS for its own domain; encryption is not identity verification.
A cached HTTP 301 redirect can make a browser keep choosing a new URL long after the original server changes its mind.
HTTP 404 means “not found”; status 410 more explicitly says a resource was intentionally removed.
An HTTP 503 can include Retry-After to tell clients when to try again instead of hammering an overloaded server.
https://example.com and https://example.com:8443 are different browser origins because their ports differ.
CORS blocks some browser JavaScript requests; the same API may still be called by a CLI or backend client.
A DNS answer with a 60-second TTL can remain cached for up to a minute before a resolver checks for changes.
A CDN can serve a cached image from a nearby edge location without contacting its original server for every visitor.
A browser can receive HTTP 304 “Not Modified” and reuse a cached file rather than downloading its contents again.
HTTP/2 can fetch several resources over one connection without opening a separate TCP connection for each.
HTTP/3 rides on QUIC over UDP, not TCP; it still provides reliable delivery at the transport layer.
A WebSocket connection begins with an HTTP handshake before switching into a two-way message channel.
Server-Sent Events let a web page receive a live stream over ordinary HTTP; browsers can reconnect automatically.
Putting a secret URL in robots.txt can advertise its location: the file is public advice to crawlers, not a security wall.
A page listed in sitemap.xml is not guaranteed to appear in Google results; indexing is a separate decision.
A web address does not require “www”: example.com and www.example.com can even point to different servers.
CSS was proposed by Håkon Wium Lie in 1994.
The first HTML specification was much simpler than modern HTML and contained no CSS.
SVG is a text-based XML format for scalable vector graphics.
The first version of Netscape Navigator was released in 1994.
Mosaic, released in 1993, helped bring graphical web browsing to mainstream users.
The original web had no built-in search engine; early visitors followed links and indexes.
Early browser favicons were usually 16×16 pixels; today one site may provide icons in several sizes.
The 'favicon.ico' convention originated with Internet Explorer 5 in 1999.
WebAssembly allows compiled code from languages such as Rust or C++ to run inside a browser sandbox.
With a service worker, a web app can load previously cached pages while the user is offline.
localStorage saves strings: storing a JavaScript object directly produces a string such as “[object Object]”.
Unlike an SVG shape, an HTML canvas drawing is generally just pixels after it has been painted.
JavaScript cannot read an HttpOnly cookie, but the browser can still send it automatically with matching requests.
One domain can publish several A records so clients may be sent toward different IPv4 addresses.
“localhost” can resolve to 127.0.0.1 or ::1, sending traffic back to the same machine.
A web server can use HTTPS on port 8443; 443 and 80 are conventions, not mandatory protocol limits.
An ETag helps a browser ask “has this file changed?” and can turn a full download into an HTTP 304 response.
In a room of just 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is better than even.
Euclid proved around 300 BC that there are infinitely many prime numbers, and his proof is still taught today.
A googol is 10 to the power of 100. The name came from Milton Sirotta, the 9-year-old nephew of mathematician Edward Kasner.
A deck of 52 cards can be ordered in 52! ways, about 8 × 10^67, so a well-shuffled deck is almost surely in an order never seen before.
The four colour theorem, proved in 1976, was the first major theorem proved with the help of a computer.
Zero is an even number: it is divisible by 2 without a remainder.
The sum of the first n odd positive numbers is n²: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16.
The sum of the angles in a Euclidean triangle is exactly 180 degrees.
The square root of 2 cannot be written as a ratio of two integers.
There are infinitely many different sizes of infinity in set theory.
The set of real numbers is uncountable, while the set of rational numbers is countable.
A Möbius strip has only one side and one boundary curve.
A Klein bottle can be immersed in 3D, but a true embedding needs four dimensions.
Euler's identity e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 connects five famous mathematical constants.
A circle has more area than any other plane shape with the same perimeter.
The decimal 0.999... is exactly equal to 1, not merely close to it.
There are five Platonic solids, and no sixth regular convex polyhedron.
A pinwheel can have rotational symmetry even when it has no mirror symmetry.
Every finite tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves.
In graph theory, a tree with n vertices has exactly n - 1 edges.
The bridges of Königsberg inspired Euler's early work on graph theory in 1736.
A perfect number equals the sum of its positive proper divisors; 6 is the smallest.
Only one even prime exists: the number 2.
Every prime greater than 3 is one more or one less than a multiple of 6.
The Fibonacci sequence begins 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5; each later term sums the previous two.
The golden ratio is irrational, approximately 1.6180339887.
Pascal's triangle contains the binomial coefficients and shows the coefficients of (a+b)^n.
A fair six-sided die has an expected roll of 3.5, even though 3.5 cannot be rolled.
The Monty Hall problem gives a 2/3 winning chance if you switch doors under its standard rules.
Two fair dice have 36 equally likely ordered outcomes, but their sums are not equally likely.
The sum 1 + 2 + ... + n equals n(n+1)/2.
A googolplex is 10 raised to the power of a googol, far too large to write in decimal on Earth.
Pi is irrational and transcendental, so it cannot satisfy any nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients.
The digits of pi never terminate and never eventually repeat.
A sphere has the smallest surface area of any solid enclosing a given volume.
If you double a cube's side length, its volume increases eightfold.
A 4D hypercube has 16 vertices, 32 edges, 24 square faces and 8 cubic cells.
The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... diverges even though its terms approach zero.
The alternating harmonic series converges to ln(2), roughly 0.693.
A prime number can contain millions of digits; no fixed upper bound on prime size exists.
A proof by contradiction assumes the opposite of the claim and derives an impossibility.
The pigeonhole principle says 11 socks in 10 drawers force at least one drawer to hold two socks.
A Sudoku puzzle has a finite number of valid completed grids: about 6.67 sextillion.
An Eulerian circuit uses every edge of a graph exactly once and returns to its start.
A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex of a graph exactly once before returning home.
The median can resist extreme outliers much better than the arithmetic mean.
A standard deviation of zero means all observed values are identical.
The binomial theorem works for every nonnegative integer exponent.
Bayes' theorem updates probabilities when new evidence arrives.
A random walk can return to its starting point many times without retracing the same path.
Venus turns so slowly that one rotation takes 243 Earth days, longer than its year of 225.
The International Space Station circles Earth about 16 times a day, so its crew sees about 16 sunrises and sunsets.
Both Voyager probes carry a gold-plated record of sounds and images from Earth, in case anyone ever finds them.
A day on Mercury lasts about 176 Earth days from sunrise to sunrise, longer than its 88-day year.
Mercury completes three rotations for every two trips around the Sun.
Venus rotates backwards compared with most planets, so the Sun rises in the west there.
Venus has a surface hot enough to melt lead, at roughly 465 degrees Celsius.
Olympus Mons is the tallest known volcano in the Solar System, but Alba Mons covers a larger area of Mars.
Mars's moon Phobos is slowly spiraling inward and may eventually break apart or crash.
The atmosphere of Mars is mostly carbon dioxide and far thinner than Earth's.
Saturn is less dense than water on average, though no ocean could hold the planet.
Saturn's rings consist mostly of countless chunks of water ice, from grains to large blocks.
Saturn's moon Titan has lakes and seas made mainly of liquid methane and ethane.
Titan has a dense nitrogen atmosphere, unusual among moons in our Solar System.
Jupiter's present Great Red Spot has been recorded since 1831; a similar spot observed in 1665 may have been a different storm.
Jupiter has no solid surface on which a spacecraft could simply land.
Jupiter's moon Europa likely hides a global liquid-water ocean below its icy crust.
Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System, even wider than Mercury.
Io, a moon of Jupiter, is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System.
Uranus spins almost on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees.
Neptune was discovered in 1846 after calculations predicted where another planet might be.
Neptune's winds can exceed 2,000 kilometres per hour.
Pluto and its moon Charon orbit a point outside Pluto, making their pairing unusual.
The Moon is moving away from Earth by about 3.8 centimetres per year.
The Moon shows nearly the same face to Earth because it is tidally locked.
Moonlight takes about 1.3 seconds to reach Earth.
Earth's atmosphere extends far beyond the altitude where astronauts orbit.
The Kármán line at 100 km is a commonly used boundary of space, not a physical wall.
The Sun contains about 99.86% of the Solar System's total mass.
The Sun is a star, and its visible surface is called the photosphere.
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth.
During a total solar eclipse, observers can see the Sun's outer corona.
A neutron star can pack more mass than the Sun into a sphere roughly the size of a city.
Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose beams can sweep past Earth like lighthouse beams.
Some white dwarfs are about Earth's size despite containing a mass comparable to the Sun's.
A black hole's event horizon is the boundary beyond which light cannot escape to distant observers.
The Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars, and our Sun is just one of them.
The nearest star to the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.24 light-years away.
A light-year measures distance, not time: it is how far light travels through vacuum in one year.
The cosmic microwave background is leftover radiation from the early universe.
The James Webb Space Telescope observes largely in infrared rather than visible light.
The Hubble Space Telescope orbits Earth, not the Sun.
The first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, launched on 4 October 1957.
Yuri Gagarin became the first human to orbit Earth in April 1961.
Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963.
The Apollo 11 astronauts left a laser reflector on the Moon that researchers can still use.
Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012, but will take centuries more to reach the Oort Cloud.
The tiny particles of a comet's tail are pushed away from the Sun by sunlight and solar wind.
A newborn has around 270 bones. Many fuse while growing up, leaving an adult with about 206.
The smallest bone in the body is the stapes in the middle ear, about 3 millimetres long.
The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy.
Humans have more than five senses: balance, the sense of where your limbs are, and temperature are senses too.
Identical twins share almost all of their DNA, but not their fingerprints.
The cornea has no blood vessels; it receives oxygen directly from air and nutrients from nearby fluids.
Red blood cells lack nuclei when mature, leaving more room for oxygen-carrying hemoglobin.
An adult human heart beats roughly 100,000 times in an average day.
Your liver can regenerate substantial lost tissue after partial surgical removal.
The human liver makes bile, which helps digest fats.
Your stomach lining replaces many surface cells within a few days.
An adult's skin covers roughly 1.5–2 square metres and is usually described as the body's largest organ by weight.
Melanin helps protect skin against ultraviolet radiation.
Fingerprints form before birth and usually remain recognizable throughout life.
The left lung has two lobes; the right has three, partly to accommodate the heart.
The diaphragm is the main muscle used in quiet breathing.
The human body contains more than 600 skeletal muscles.
The masseter is one of the muscles responsible for closing the jaw.
The tongue is made of several muscles working together, not a single muscle.
Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
Adult humans typically have 32 permanent teeth, including wisdom teeth.
The human eye contains a natural blind spot where the optic nerve exits the retina.
The lens of your eye changes shape to focus on objects at different distances.
Your pupils change size in response to light, but also to some emotions and medications.
The inner ear contains semicircular canals that help detect rotational head movement.
The cochlea converts sound vibrations into signals sent toward the brain.
The human hand has 27 bones, including eight small wrist bones.
Nerves can carry signals from the spinal cord to muscles at speeds exceeding 100 metres per second.
The brain and spinal cord together form the central nervous system.
Most neurons communicate across tiny gaps called synapses rather than physically touching.
The cerebellum is especially important for coordination and motor learning.
Cerebrospinal fluid cushions the brain and spinal cord.
A widely cited estimate places about 86 billion neurons in the human brain, though the true total remains uncertain.
Your sleep cycles repeatedly include both REM and non-REM stages.
REM sleep is associated with rapid eye movements and vivid dreams.
During sleep, the brain helps consolidate some kinds of memory.
The kidneys filter blood and help balance water, salts and blood pressure.
Each kidney contains roughly a million filtering units called nephrons.
The spleen filters blood and participates in immune responses.
Platelets are cell fragments that help blood clot after injury.
Human blood is red because of hemoglobin; veins only look blue through skin.
A single haploid human genome contains roughly 3 billion DNA base pairs; exact counts vary by reference assembly.
Mitochondria produce much of the ATP that powers cells.
Your cells share almost the same DNA but can behave differently because different genes are active.
Human bones are living tissue that is continually broken down and rebuilt.
Your gut is home to a complex microbial community, often called the gut microbiota.
A baby's kneecap begins largely as cartilage and ossifies during childhood.
The vestibular system continues sensing balance even when your eyes are shut.
Your body generates heat as a by-product of metabolism, even when you are resting.
Unlike many mammals, humans have abundant sweat glands that help cool the body by evaporation.
An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, which carries oxygen with copper-based hemocyanin.
One of the largest living things is a honey fungus in Oregon, spreading underground across about 9 square kilometres.
Pando, a grove of quaking aspen in Utah, is a single organism: some 47,000 stems on one root system.
Some tardigrades can survive drying out by entering a near-dormant state called a tun.
Tardigrades can survive exposure to the vacuum of space under certain conditions.
Axolotls can regenerate damaged limbs, spinal cord tissue and parts of several organs.
A starfish can regrow lost arms, and some species can regenerate much of the body.
The immortal jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from its adult stage to an earlier life stage.
A mantis shrimp's strike can generate cavitation bubbles in water.
The mantis shrimp is known for unusually complex eyes with many types of photoreceptors.
Bees can communicate the direction and distance of food using a waggle dance.
Some ants cultivate fungi as their food source, effectively practicing agriculture.
Leafcutter ants don't eat the leaves they cut; they use them to grow fungus.
Termites maintain temperature and ventilation inside elaborate mounds.
A male seahorse carries developing embryos in a specialized brood pouch.
Clownfish can change sex; the dominant individual in a group is typically female.
Male emperor penguins incubate eggs on their feet during the Antarctic winter.
Penguin feathers provide insulation and waterproofing in icy seas.
Hummingbirds can hover in place and fly backwards.
An albatross can glide for long periods by using changes in wind speed above ocean waves.
Some migratory birds navigate using Earth's magnetic field.
The Arctic tern migrates between Arctic and Antarctic regions each year.
The peregrine falcon can reach extreme speeds during a hunting dive, called a stoop.
A platypus lays eggs, even though it is a mammal.
A platypus can detect electric signals produced by prey in water.
Male platypuses have venomous spurs on their hind legs.
Echidnas are egg-laying mammals that feed on ants and termites.
A blue whale's heart can weigh well over 100 kilograms.
Blue whales are the largest animals known to have existed on Earth.
Elephants can detect low-frequency vibrations through their feet.
A giraffe has seven neck vertebrae, the same number as most other mammals.
Some sharks must keep swimming to move enough water over their gills; others can rest.
Greenland sharks are exceptionally long-lived, with estimated lifespans reaching centuries.
The mimic octopus can imitate the appearance and movements of other sea animals.
Some cuttlefish rapidly change their skin patterns using specialized pigment cells.
Coral reefs are built largely by colonies of tiny animals called coral polyps.
Coral bleaching occurs when stressed corals lose symbiotic algae or their pigments.
Mangrove trees can tolerate saltwater and help protect coastlines from erosion.
A Venus flytrap closes when trigger hairs are touched in a particular sequence.
The giant water lily has leaves reinforced with a lattice of strong ribs.
Baobab trees can store substantial amounts of water in their trunks.
Some bamboo species can grow more than half a metre in one day under ideal conditions.
A single mycelium can connect many mushrooms, which are just the fungus's fruiting bodies.
Bioluminescent dinoflagellates can make breaking ocean waves glow blue at night.
Fireflies produce light through a chemical reaction involving luciferin.
The bombardier beetle ejects a hot chemical spray from its abdomen to deter predators.
Some spiders travel through the air on strands of silk in a behavior called ballooning.
The wood frog can survive partial freezing in winter by protecting its cells with glucose.
Some frogs carry tadpoles on their backs to small pools of water.
Oysters can change sex during their lives, depending on species and conditions.
Junk email is called spam after a 1970 Monty Python sketch in which Vikings in a café drown out all talk by singing "Spam".
The web cookie is named after the magic cookie, an older term for a token a program receives and passes back unchanged.
The word robot comes from Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R.; his brother Josef suggested it, from the Czech robota, forced labour.
"Bit", short for binary digit, first appeared in print in Claude Shannon's 1948 paper, which credited John Tukey with the word.
Pixel blends "picture element". The word first appeared in print in 1965.
The word 'algorithm' comes from the name of the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
'Algebra' comes from the Arabic word al-jabr in the title of al-Khwarizmi's book.
The word 'salary' is linked to Latin salarium, but the claim that Romans were paid in salt is disputed.
'Quarantine' derives from Italian quaranta, meaning forty, referring to a historical 40-day isolation period.
The word 'clue' comes from 'clew', a ball of thread associated with the story of Theseus.
'Candidate' comes from Latin candidatus, referring to the white clothing worn by Roman office-seekers.
The word 'alphabet' comes from the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta.
'Ampersand' comes from a phrase treating '&' as 'and per se and'.
The 'at' sign was used in commercial records long before it became an email symbol.
'Emoji' comes from Japanese e (picture) and moji (character), not from 'emotion'.
The word 'meme' was coined by Richard Dawkins in 1976 for a unit of cultural transmission.
'Bluetooth' is named after Harald Bluetooth, a tenth-century king of Denmark.
The Bluetooth logo combines runes associated with the initials of Harald Bluetooth.
'Wi-Fi' is a brand name, not an official abbreviation of 'Wireless Fidelity'.
The term 'debugging' appeared in 1945 aviation writing about aircraft engines and cameras, before becoming a staple of computing.
'Avatar' comes from a Sanskrit word meaning descent, especially of a deity into earthly form.
'Robot' and 'robotics' have different literary histories; Isaac Asimov popularized the latter.
'Cyberspace' was coined in fiction by William Gibson in the early 1980s.
'Podcast' blends 'iPod' and 'broadcast', even though podcasts never required an iPod.
'Blog' is a shortening of 'weblog', meaning a log kept on the web.
'Wiki' comes from Hawaiian wiki, meaning quick.
'Captcha' is an acronym involving 'Completely Automated Public Turing test'.
'Laser' stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.
'Radar' stands for Radio Detection and Ranging.
'Sonar' stands for Sound Navigation and Ranging.
'Scuba' comes from Self-Contained Underwater Breathing Apparatus.
'GIF' stands for Graphics Interchange Format and was introduced by CompuServe in 1987.
'JPEG' is named after the Joint Photographic Experts Group, the committee behind the standard.
'PNG' stands for Portable Network Graphics and was designed as a patent-free alternative to GIF.
'USB' means Universal Serial Bus, not 'Universal Storage Bus'.
'RAM' means Random-Access Memory; it refers to access patterns, not randomness in data.
'ROM' stands for Read-Only Memory, though some ROM technologies can be rewritten.
'HTTP' stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol, while HTML is HyperText Markup Language.
'Unix' was a pun on Multics, the earlier operating system that inspired it.
'Linux' takes its name from Linus Torvalds and Unix.
'Google' is a play on 'googol', the mathematical name for 10^100.
'Sandbox' is a metaphor for an isolated space where experiments cannot easily damage the rest of a system.
'Bug' can mean a programming flaw, but its technological use predates Grace Hopper's famous moth.
The particle name 'quark' was borrowed from a phrase in James Joyce's novel Finnegans Wake.
'Television' combines Greek tele (far) with Latin visio (seeing).
'Telephone' combines Greek roots meaning far and sound.
The English word 'cipher' traces back through Arabic sifr, meaning empty or zero.
In 1995, astronomers found 51 Pegasi b, the first confirmed planet around a Sun-like star; its year lasts only about four days.
The late-1990s discovery that cosmic expansion is accelerating overturned the expectation that gravity should slow it down.
In 2012, CERN announced a particle consistent with the long-sought Higgs boson after decades of searching.
In September 2015, LIGO first detected gravitational waves from merging black holes; the result was announced in 2016.
In 2017, astronomers detected gravitational waves and light from the same neutron-star merger, opening multi-messenger astronomy.
The first black-hole image, released in 2019, showed a bright ring around the shadow of the object at the heart of galaxy M87.
In 2022, astronomers revealed the first image of Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way.
In 2022, a fusion experiment produced 3.15 megajoules of fusion energy from 2.05 MJ of laser energy delivered to its target.
IceCube reported evidence in 2013 of high-energy neutrinos arriving from beyond the Solar System.
In 2018, IceCube observations linked a high-energy neutrino to a distant blazar, a galaxy with an active jet pointed toward Earth.
Graphene was isolated in 2004 using ordinary adhesive tape to peel layers from graphite; it is only one atom thick.
The first Bose–Einstein condensates in dilute atomic gases were produced in 1995 at temperatures near absolute zero.
In 2009, scientists imaged the chemical structure of a single pentacene molecule using an atomic force microscope.
In 2016, the names nihonium, moscovium, tennessine and oganesson were approved for four newly discovered elements.
In 2003, physicists measured bismuth-209 radioactivity with a half-life vastly longer than the age of the universe.
In 2012, researchers demonstrated CRISPR-Cas9 as a programmable way to cut DNA at a chosen sequence.
In 2023, the UK approved Casgevy, the first licensed treatment using CRISPR gene editing.
In 2022, researchers published the first gapless sequence of a human genome, filling regions left unfinished in 2003.
The 2023 human pangenome draft combined genomes from 47 people instead of relying on one reference sequence.
In 2023, scientists assembled the first complete sequence of a human Y chromosome, the last chromosome to be fully sequenced.
The Human Genome Project announced an essentially complete sequence in 2003, although difficult gaps remained for two decades.
In 2024, scientists mapped an adult fruit fly brain: nearly 140,000 neurons connected by over 50 million synapses.
In 2023, researchers mapped a fruit fly larva’s brain, identifying 3,016 neurons and about 548,000 connections.
In 2010, DNA from a finger-bone fragment revealed the Denisovans, an ancient human group previously unknown from fossils alone.
In 2022, DNA recovered from northern Greenland revealed an ecosystem from about two million years ago.
A 2016 study estimated some Greenland sharks could live for centuries, with the oldest sampled individual estimated near 392 years.
Scientists described a giant bacterium in 2022 whose individual cells can be visible to the naked eye.
In 2019, researchers identified Homo luzonensis from fossils found in a Philippine cave.
In 2015, researchers formally described Homo naledi from a remarkable concentration of fossils in a South African cave.
In 2006, Shinya Yamanaka’s team showed that adult mouse cells could be reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells.
In 2017, astronomers revealed seven Earth-sized planets orbiting the tiny star TRAPPIST-1.
In 2016, astronomers announced Proxima Centauri b, a planet around the nearest star to the Sun.
Discovered in 2017, ʻOumuamua became the first confirmed visitor to our Solar System from interstellar space.
Comet 2I/Borisov, discovered in 2019, was the first confirmed interstellar comet, entering from beyond the Solar System.
Comet 3I/ATLAS, spotted in July 2025, became the third confirmed interstellar object detected passing through our Solar System.
On 19 April 2021, NASA’s Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
In April 2021, an experiment called MOXIE made oxygen from the carbon-dioxide-rich air of Mars.
In 2022, NASA’s DART spacecraft deliberately hit Dimorphos and shortened its orbit by about 32 minutes.
In 2023, NASA returned 121.6 grams of rocks and dust from asteroid Bennu to Earth.
In 2020, Japan’s Hayabusa2 mission returned about 5.4 grams of material from asteroid Ryugu.
In 2014, the Philae probe made humanity’s first landing on a comet, touching down on 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko.
In 2022, Webb detected carbon dioxide in exoplanet WASP-39 b’s atmosphere using a signature in infrared starlight.
In 2022, Webb detected sulfur dioxide in WASP-39 b’s atmosphere, evidence of chemistry driven by starlight.
ESA’s Euclid space telescope released its first full-color images in November 2023, showing galaxies with unusual clarity.
In 2005, the Huygens probe landed on Titan, the first spacecraft touchdown on a world in the outer Solar System.
Cassini found active jets of icy particles erupting from Saturn’s moon Enceladus in 2005.
In 2019, NASA’s InSight recorded its first likely marsquake, revealing seismic activity on another planet.
In 2015, New Horizons revealed mountains of water ice on Pluto, upending expectations for such a distant world.
In 2024, China’s Chang’e-6 returned the first samples ever collected from the far side of the Moon.
Scientists reported in 2023 that ancient footprints at White Sands support humans living in North America 21,000–23,000 years ago.
AES always encrypts 128-bit blocks, even when its key is 256 bits long; a larger key does not mean a larger block.
RSA was publicly described in 1977; its name is the initials of Rivest, Shamir and Adleman.
Diffie and Hellman published public-key exchange in 1976: two strangers can agree on a secret without sending it directly.
Change a single input bit and a good cryptographic hash can alter roughly half of the bits in its digest.
In 2017, researchers published two different PDF files with the same SHA-1 hash, demonstrating a real collision.
SHA-256 produces a 256-bit digest, often displayed as 64 hexadecimal characters.
MD5 is considered cryptographically broken because attackers can construct collisions.
In 2008, researchers used MD5 collisions to create a rogue certificate authority certificate accepted by some software.
A 256-bit hash resists generic collision search at roughly 2^128 work, because of the birthday paradox.
Two users can choose the same password yet have different stored hashes when each password has a unique salt.
Password hashing can be deliberately memory-hungry, making mass guessing expensive even on powerful GPUs.
Argon2 won the Password Hashing Competition in 2015.
A one-time pad provides perfect secrecy if its random key is truly random, secret and never reused.
Reuse the same one-time-pad key for two messages and XORing their ciphertexts cancels the key out.
Julius Caesar’s name survives in a cipher with only 25 meaningful shift keys for the English alphabet.
The Vigenère cipher was long considered difficult to break, but repeated-key patterns gave cryptanalysts a foothold.
The German Enigma machine used rotating wheels to create changing substitution alphabets.
RSA public keys can be published openly; knowing the public key need not reveal the secret needed to decrypt.
A digital signature can be checked with a public key without giving verifiers the private key that produced it.
A modern TLS handshake can agree on fresh session keys even though client and server have never met before.
With forward secrecy, stealing a website’s private key tomorrow need not decrypt the TLS traffic recorded today.
On an unsecured network, a man-in-the-middle can present two different conversations while both endpoints think they talk directly.
A recorded request might be valid a second time too; anti-replay designs use counters, timestamps or nonces.
A nonce need not be secret; in schemes like AES-GCM, what matters is not repeating it with the same key.
Reusing a nonce with AES-GCM can catastrophically weaken confidentiality and authenticity.
HMAC lets two systems detect message tampering using a shared secret without encrypting the message itself.
Rainbow tables become far less useful when every password hash includes its own random salt.
A password and a PIN are both knowledge factors; adding a second password does not create true two-factor authentication.
Many authenticator apps show a fresh six-digit code every 30 seconds, computed from time and a secret.
Passkeys can bind authentication to a specific website, making stolen lookalike login pages much less useful.
WebAuthn can authenticate with a device-held private key without sending that private key to the website.
The classic SQL injection input `' OR 1=1 --` tries to turn data into part of a database query.
Parameterized SQL keeps a malicious-looking string as data: `' OR 1=1 --` no longer changes the query logic.
A forum comment can become a script execution attack if a site inserts its HTML into a page without safe handling.
Browsers attach cookies automatically; without CSRF defenses, a malicious page may trigger a logged-in action elsewhere.
The 1988 Morris worm exploited a buffer overflow in Unix's finger service among other weaknesses.
ASLR randomizes memory locations, forcing some exploits to guess addresses rather than rely on a fixed layout.
A browser sandbox can let untrusted code run while still blocking direct access to many operating-system resources.
A service that only needs to read one table should not have permission to delete the entire database.
A user on the company Wi-Fi is not automatically trusted under zero-trust security principles.
A certificate for a lookalike domain can be technically valid; HTTPS does not prove a site is honest.
Certificate Transparency makes issued TLS certificates searchable in public logs, helping expose suspicious issuance.
Many hardware security modules can perform signing without ever exporting the private key they protect.
Attackers have extracted secrets by measuring tiny differences in processing time rather than reading stored data.
Spectre exploits speculative execution to leak information across security boundaries.
Meltdown exploited certain processors' handling of out-of-order execution and memory access.
The Heartbleed bug exposed memory contents from some OpenSSL servers and clients in 2014.
In 2017, the KRACK attack showed that some WPA2 Wi-Fi connections could be attacked by forcing key reinstallation.
A zero-day can be exploited before its developer has a patch; the term describes a timing problem, not a severity score.
A stolen password alone need not unlock an account protected by a properly configured independent second factor.
The Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 after one team used imperial units and another expected metric units.
The Ariane 5 rocket failed on its first flight in 1996 after a numeric conversion overflow.
In 1962, Mariner 1 was destroyed shortly after launch when its guidance system malfunctioned.
A 2009 Google blacklist update briefly marked nearly every search result as potentially harmful, including Google itself.
In 2008, Debian discovered that a tiny change to OpenSSL had reduced cryptographic randomness in generated keys for almost two years.
The 2003 Northeast blackout was worsened by a software alarm failure at a power utility.
A faulty software update grounded many flights and disrupted businesses during the 2024 CrowdStrike outage.
The Knight Capital trading failure in 2012 caused huge losses within about 45 minutes.
A 2017 Amazon S3 outage began with an incorrect command that removed more servers than intended.
The 2016 Dyn attack disrupted major websites by targeting a DNS provider with a DDoS attack.
The SQL Slammer worm infected vulnerable servers and disrupted networks in 2003.
The WannaCry ransomware attack spread worldwide in 2017, exploiting an SMB vulnerability.
The 2017 NotPetya attack spread destructive malware while masquerading as ransomware.
The ILOVEYOU worm spread in 2000 through email attachments disguised as love letters.
The Code Red worm exploited a buffer overflow in Microsoft IIS in 2001.
The Log4Shell vulnerability in Log4j became public in December 2021.
A missing validation check in Apple's 2014 'goto fail' bug weakened TLS certificate verification.
The Pentium FDIV bug affected division results on some early Intel Pentium processors.
The Y2K problem arose because many systems stored years using only two digits.
Some systems may face issues in 2038 when signed 32-bit Unix timestamps overflow.
A leap-second bug in Linux caused high CPU usage on some systems in 2012.
In 2012, a leap-day bug caused certain Microsoft Azure services to fail.
In 2010, a software bug forced some PlayStation 3 consoles offline on 1 March.
A 1990 AT&T telephone network outage was triggered by a flaw in updated switching software.
The 1999 Mars Polar Lander may have shut down its engines early when landing-leg vibration was mistaken for touchdown.
In 2019, Cloudflare's firewall rule triggered a CPU spike after a regex ran too slowly, temporarily disrupting its services.
The Hubble telescope initially suffered from a misshaped mirror caused by faulty test equipment.
Hubble's optical flaw was corrected using instruments installed by astronauts in 1993.
In 2004, Mars rover Spirit entered a reboot loop due to a flash-memory problem; NASA recovered it by deleting thousands of files.
In 2013, Mars rover Curiosity switched to its backup computer after a flash-memory fault affected the main one.
In 2014, Apple quickly withdrew iOS 8.0.1 after it disabled cellular service and Touch ID on some iPhone 6 models.
A 2010 Bitcoin overflow bug briefly created over 184 billion bitcoins before the network was fixed.
The DAO exploit of 2016 led to a controversial Ethereum blockchain hard fork.
In 2023, a Redis-related bug temporarily let some ChatGPT users see other users' conversation titles.
GitLab's 2017 database incident became well known for its publicly streamed recovery effort.
Apple Maps launched in 2012 with widely reported map errors, leading Apple to issue a public apology.
In 2018, GitHub survived a DDoS attack peaking near 1.35 terabits per second, amplified through exposed Memcached servers.
The 2010 Flash Crash saw US markets plunge and partially recover within minutes.
An incorrect BGP advertisement can redirect or disrupt internet traffic worldwide.
In 2008, a mistaken BGP route intended to block YouTube in Pakistan disrupted access elsewhere.
The 2019 Google Cloud outage followed a configuration change that triggered network congestion.
A single badly configured regular expression can cause a service-denial vulnerability called ReDoS.
An unbounded retry loop can turn a small outage into a traffic-amplifying retry storm.
A race condition can make two concurrent requests both believe they bought the last available item.
Two transactions can deadlock if each holds a resource the other needs; databases often resolve this by aborting one transaction.
In June 2021, a software bug triggered by a valid configuration change caused a major outage across Fastly's CDN.
In 2021, a network configuration update made Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp unreachable for hours.
Binary search can locate an item in 1,024 sorted entries using at most 11 comparisons.
Binary search needs only about 20 comparisons to search a million sorted items in the worst case.
Double a sorted list from one million to two million entries and binary search needs only about one extra comparison.
Merge sort keeps O(n log n) worst-case time even when the input is in reverse order.
A naive quicksort that always chooses the first element as pivot can hit O(n²) on already sorted input.
Unlike naive quicksort, heapsort guarantees O(n log n) comparisons even on adversarial input.
A poorly designed hash function can turn expected O(1) lookups into long chains of collisions.
A Bloom filter can say “definitely absent” or “possibly present”, but never promise that an item exists.
A Bloom filter can answer millions of membership queries using only a compact bit array, not the original records.
Autocomplete engines can use a trie to find all words beginning with “pre” without checking every dictionary word.
Morse code needs gaps between letters; prefix-free codes can be decoded without separators.
Huffman coding assigns frequent symbols short bit strings, reducing average message length without losing data.
ZIP-style Lempel–Ziv compressors can store repeated text as references to earlier occurrences instead of copying it.
A lossless compressor must sometimes enlarge data: there are more 1,024-bit strings than shorter strings available to encode them.
No lossless compressor can make every possible input shorter than it started.
An algorithm described as O(1) can still run slowly; the notation hides constant factors.
An algorithm can use O(1) additional space while still allocating a fixed-size buffer with thousands of bytes.
An algorithm with O(n²) work may still win on tiny inputs because constants matter.
Dijkstra’s shortest-path method fails with negative edge weights unless extra conditions or algorithms are used.
Bellman–Ford can discover a reachable negative cycle because improving distances never stops.
A* can return an optimal path when its heuristic never overestimates the remaining cost.
Breadth-first search finds shortest routes in an unweighted maze by exploring all spots one step away before two steps away.
Depth-first search can overflow the call stack on a huge graph if implemented recursively without safeguards.
If a dependency graph contains a cycle, no topological ordering can put every prerequisite first.
Kahn’s algorithm reveals dependency cycles when some nodes remain after every zero-indegree node is removed.
Union–find can merge groups almost instantly in practice, even across millions of elements, using path compression.
Kruskal’s minimum-spanning-tree algorithm sorts edges and rejects any edge that would create a cycle.
Dynamic programming can turn naive exponential Fibonacci recursion into linear work by remembering earlier results.
Memoized Fibonacci computes each needed value once, instead of repeatedly building the same recursion tree.
A greedy knapsack choice can fail spectacularly: taking the best value-per-weight item may block a better combination.
For only 20 cities, there are over 60 quadrillion possible round trips if direction and start are fixed.
The traveling-salesperson decision problem is NP-complete, even though any proposed route can be checked quickly.
No one has proved whether P equals NP, despite a million-dollar prize for resolving the question.
No algorithm can correctly decide whether every possible program will eventually halt.
A stable sort keeps equal-price orders in their previous date order, making multi-key sorting predictable.
No comparison sort can guarantee fewer than roughly n log₂(n) comparisons for arbitrary distinct keys as n grows.
Counting sort can beat comparison sorting when the input keys come from a small known integer range.
Radix sort can order fixed-length IDs without comparing whole IDs as comparison sorts do.
Reservoir sampling can pick one fair random item from a billion-item stream while storing just one candidate.
A sliding-window protocol can keep multiple packets in flight instead of waiting for one acknowledgment at a time.
Knuth–Morris–Pratt avoids rescanning text characters after a failed pattern match by reusing prefix information.
Rabin–Karp hashes each text window; it still checks candidate matches because two different strings can hash alike.
A rolling hash can update after a one-character slide without hashing the entire window from scratch.
Consistent hashing can add a cache node while remapping far fewer keys than a simple modulo hash would.
Merkle trees let systems prove one file chunk belongs to a large dataset using only a small path of hashes.
B-trees use many keys per node so a database can navigate huge indexes with comparatively few disk reads.
A red–black tree avoids growing into a linked list by recoloring and rotating nodes after updates.
A monotonic stack can solve nearest-greater-element queries for an entire array in O(n) time.
A skip list uses randomized “express lanes” to search in expected O(log n) time.
An LRU cache may evict a rare but expensive result just because it has not been requested recently.
GPS satellite clocks need corrections from both special and general relativity to stay accurate.
The metre is defined using light: in vacuum, light travels exactly 299,792,458 metres in one second.
No matter how much fuel you add, an object with nonzero rest mass cannot reach light speed in vacuum.
A near-light-speed traveler can age less than someone who remains on Earth; the effect has been measured with clocks.
An atomic clock on a mountain ticks slightly faster than one at sea level because of gravitational time dilation.
The Sun converts about four million tonnes of mass into energy every second, illustrating E = mc².
Gravity can bend light into arcs and even rings when a distant galaxy is aligned behind a massive foreground object.
A glass prism can split white light into colors because each wavelength bends by a different amount.
Even when fired one at a time, electrons can build up an interference pattern in a double-slit experiment.
A beam of light exerts a tiny force on a surface; solar sails use photons’ momentum instead of carrying fuel.
Einstein’s 1921 Nobel Prize recognized his explanation of the photoelectric effect, not relativity.
A heated metal object glows dull red before orange and then white as its temperature rises.
Absolute zero is −273.15 °C, but no finite sequence of cooling operations can bring a system exactly to 0 K.
A hot cup of coffee cools in a cold room; the reverse does not occur spontaneously on a macroscopic scale.
A glass of ice water can melt while room temperature stays steady; the total entropy of the isolated whole still rises.
A machine that turned ambient heat entirely into work in a cycle would violate the second law of thermodynamics.
Ice floats because water expands when freezing; that helps lakes freeze from the top rather than solidifying bottom-first.
Water is densest near 4 °C, so colder water can remain at the surface while deeper lake water stays above freezing.
Some superconducting materials carry electric current without measurable DC resistance below a critical temperature.
A superconductor can levitate a magnet by expelling or pinning magnetic fields, depending on the material.
Graphene can conduct electricity extremely well despite being only one atom thick.
A dramatic explosion in a perfect vacuum would be silent to a distant listener: sound requires matter to travel through.
An ambulance siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower after passing because of the Doppler effect.
A sonic boom can be heard long after a supersonic aircraft has flown overhead; the shock wave travels outward.
A skydiver changes terminal speed by changing body position: spreading out increases drag.
Tiny MEMS gyroscopes in smartphones sense rotation using vibrating structures, not spinning mechanical wheels.
For small swings, a pendulum’s timing barely depends on how far you pulled it back.
Foucault’s 1851 pendulum experiment let people watch evidence of Earth’s rotation indoors.
The Coriolis effect shapes hurricanes but is far too weak to dictate which way water swirls in an ordinary sink.
Going about 10 metres underwater adds roughly one atmosphere of pressure on top of the air pressure above.
A steel ship floats because it displaces water whose weight matches the ship’s weight, not because steel is light.
An aircraft can generate lift upside down if its angle of attack and flight conditions are suitable.
Microwaves do not inherently cook food from the inside out; penetration depth depends on the food’s properties.
An induction cooktop can stay relatively cool while a suitable metal pan heats from induced electric currents.
An LED produces light directly in a semiconductor junction, unlike a bulb that heats a filament until it glows.
Many gas lighters use piezoelectric crystals: pressing a mechanism creates enough voltage for a spark.
Quantum tunneling helps explain how fusion can occur in the Sun at temperatures below classical barrier expectations.
Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle is not just bad instruments: certain pairs of quantum properties lack arbitrary joint precision.
An electron in an atom occupies a probability cloud, not a little planet-like orbit around the nucleus.
Measuring a qubit forces an ordinary result; superposition does not mean reading two classical answers at once.
Experiments violating Bell inequalities rule out broad classes of local hidden-variable explanations for quantum correlations.
Entangled particles can correlate across huge distances, but that correlation cannot send controllable messages faster than light.
In the Casimir effect, two uncharged plates can attract when placed extremely close together in a vacuum.
A live frog was levitated in a strong magnetic field in a famous demonstration of diamagnetism.
Physicists have searched for isolated magnetic monopoles for decades without an accepted detection.
Lightning heats nearby air so suddenly that the expanding pressure wave becomes thunder.
Sunsets look red because sunlight travels farther through air, scattering away much of the blue light.
A second rainbow reverses the color order of the first because sunlight reflects twice inside the droplets.
Polarized sunglasses cut reflections from roads or water by suppressing strongly polarized glare.
Before the 2019 SI revision, the triple point of water helped define the kelvin; today the Boltzmann constant does.
In a famous “door study”, some people failed to notice that the stranger they spoke with had been swapped for another person.
In the “invisible gorilla” experiment, many viewers counting basketball passes failed to notice a gorilla walking through.
Try saying the ink color of the word “BLUE” printed in red: the Stroop effect makes the mismatch harder to ignore.
Watch a face say “ga” while hearing “ba” and you may perceive a third syllable: the McGurk effect.
Stroke a fake hand and a hidden real hand in sync, and some people start feeling that the rubber hand is theirs.
In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two equal lines can look different in length just because the arrowheads point differently.
Everyone has a natural blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the eye; the brain usually fills the missing patch unnoticed.
People can feel an itch or even movement in a limb that is no longer present: a phantom-limb experience.
Placebo responses can change perceived pain even when a pill contains no active pain-relieving ingredient.
A warning about side effects can increase reported symptoms even when the treatment is inert: a nocebo response.
When reviewing evidence, people often notice supportive examples more readily than equally relevant contradictory ones.
In experiments, even an arbitrary starting number can influence the price someone later estimates.
Losing €20 can feel worse than finding €20 feels good, though the size of this asymmetry varies by context.
The same treatment described as “90% survive” or “10% die” can prompt different decisions despite identical odds.
People sometimes sit through a boring film only because they already paid for the ticket: the sunk-cost trap.
A dramatic viral story can make a rare event feel common simply because it is easy to remember.
A strong first impression can spill over into unrelated ratings, such as judging a friendly person as more competent.
The Dunning–Kruger effect is often oversimplified; the original research concerned calibration of ability judgments.
After learning a result, people often feel they “knew it all along”, even when their earlier prediction was uncertain.
A small stain on your shirt may feel obvious to everyone, but the spotlight effect makes us overestimate others’ attention.
Hearing a tune repeatedly can make it more appealing even when it seemed unremarkable the first time.
People may demand more money to sell a mug they own than they would have offered to buy the identical mug.
An unpleasant experience that ends less painfully may be remembered more favorably, even if it lasted longer.
A 2025 meta-analysis found little consistent evidence that interrupted tasks are remembered better, challenging the classic Zeigarnik effect.
Working memory is often estimated at roughly four chunks of information, not the old universal “seven items” rule.
A ten-digit telephone number is easier to hold in mind when grouped into meaningful chunks.
Reviewing notes across several days usually beats one long cramming session for long-term recall.
Quizzing yourself can strengthen later memory more than simply rereading the same material.
Going without enough sleep can slow reaction time even if someone feels surprisingly alert.
Your body’s internal clocks help schedule sleep, hormones and temperature across an approximately 24-hour cycle.
The brain’s suprachiasmatic nucleus uses light signals from the eyes to help keep daily rhythms aligned.
People with aphantasia may know what an apple looks like without being able to picture it voluntarily in the mind’s eye.
Some people consistently experience particular colors when reading letters or numbers, a form of synesthesia.
A person with face blindness may recognize a friend’s voice but not the friend’s face.
Capgras delusion involves believing that a familiar person has been replaced by an impostor.
Déjà vu can make an entirely new moment feel strangely familiar without providing a real memory of it.
Recalling a memory is reconstruction, not playback; the details you remember can change over time.
In memory experiments, asking how fast cars “smashed” rather than “hit” changed estimated speeds.
Confident testimony is not always accurate: people can develop vivid memories of events that never occurred.
A word can feel milliseconds away from recall for minutes in the familiar tip-of-the-tongue state.
Show one eye vertical stripes and the other horizontal stripes, and perception may alternate between them.
The Necker cube can appear to flip orientation while the drawing itself never changes.
Mirror neurons were discovered in monkeys during studies of action observation and execution.
At a noisy party, you can follow one conversation while other voices form an indistinct background.
Railway-track perspective can make two identical lines look different in size: the Ponzo illusion.
A familiar smell can instantly revive detailed autobiographical memories, a phenomenon nicknamed the Proust effect.
After several minutes in a perfume shop, the first scent may seem to fade even though it is still present.
Some people without conscious vision can still respond to light in their daily sleep-wake rhythms.
People often estimate the duration of an unpleasant wait differently from its actual clock time.
In the Simon effect, responding to a left-side stimulus with a right-hand key can take longer even when location is irrelevant.
Gallium melts at about 29.8 degrees Celsius, so a warm hand can melt a small piece.
Mercury is a metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature.
Bromine is one of the few elements that is liquid at room temperature, and the only liquid nonmetal.
Tungsten has the highest melting point of any pure metal, about 3,422 degrees Celsius.
Diamond and graphite are both made of carbon atoms arranged in different structures.
Diamond is extremely hard, but it can still fracture under a sufficiently strong impact.
Graphite conducts electricity despite being a form of pure carbon.
Carbon can form chains, rings and networks, helping explain the diversity of organic molecules.
A buckyball is a molecule of 60 carbon atoms arranged like a soccer ball.
Helium was identified in the Sun's spectrum before it was isolated on Earth.
The word 'helium' comes from Helios, the Greek personification of the Sun.
Neon lights glow reddish-orange when an electric discharge excites neon gas.
Other colors of advertising 'neon' signs often use gases or phosphors other than neon.
Argon makes up nearly one percent of Earth's dry atmosphere.
Oxygen is paramagnetic, meaning it is attracted by a magnetic field.
Ozone consists of three oxygen atoms, rather than the two in ordinary oxygen gas.
Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide and changes directly into gas at normal atmospheric pressure.
Solid carbon dioxide doesn't leave a puddle because it sublimates under ordinary room conditions.
Water has unusually high surface tension partly because of hydrogen bonding.
A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Salt can lower the freezing point of water, helping melt ice on roads.
A solution with pH 3 has ten times the hydrogen ion activity of one with pH 4.
The pH scale is logarithmic, so a shift of one unit represents a tenfold change in activity.
Universal indicator changes color depending on a solution's acidity or alkalinity.
Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic solutions and pink in many basic solutions.
Vinegar's sharp taste comes largely from acetic acid.
Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when it reacts with suitable acids.
A 'hot ice' demonstration uses supersaturated sodium acetate that crystallizes when triggered.
Rust is a mixture of iron oxides and hydroxides formed during iron corrosion.
Stainless steel resists corrosion partly because chromium forms a thin protective oxide layer.
Aluminium quickly forms a thin oxide layer that protects the underlying metal.
Sodium reacts vigorously with water, producing hydrogen and heat.
Potassium is so reactive that it is typically stored away from water and oxygen.
Gold is unusually resistant to corrosion, which helps explain why ancient gold objects survive.
Copper develops a green patina when exposed to certain atmospheric conditions over time.
A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed overall by that reaction.
Enzymes are biological catalysts that accelerate reactions in living organisms.
The Maillard reaction produces many browned flavors when sugars react with amino compounds during cooking.
Caramelization is a set of reactions that occur when sugars are heated.
The smell of rain on dry soil is often associated with geosmin made by microorganisms.
The distinctive smell of freshly cut grass comes partly from volatile green leaf compounds.
Glass is an amorphous solid, not a liquid that slowly flows at room temperature.
Aerogels are extremely porous solids that can be remarkably light.
Silica aerogel can be mostly empty space while still retaining a solid structure.
Kevlar is a high-strength synthetic fibre used in protective materials.
Teflon is a trade name for PTFE, a polymer with low friction and strong chemical resistance.
Superglue uses cyanoacrylates that polymerize rapidly in the presence of moisture.
Chemical bonds store potential energy, but breaking a bond itself requires energy input.
Noble gases are not perfectly inert: compounds of xenon, such as xenon tetrafluoride, exist.
Chess has more possible game sequences than can be enumerated by brute force with present-day computers.
The chessboard's 64 squares can be colored using only two colors so adjacent squares differ.
The knight is the only chess piece that can jump over other pieces.
A standard chess game begins with 32 pieces on 64 squares.
A chess bishop always stays on squares of the same color throughout a game.
In chess, a stalemate is a draw, even when one player has overwhelming material.
En passant is a special pawn capture that is legal only immediately after a qualifying two-square move.
The rules of modern chess evolved over centuries from earlier games such as shatranj.
Go is played by placing stones on the intersections of a grid rather than inside its squares.
A standard Go board has 19 by 19 lines, making 361 intersection points.
Go has a simple set of basic rules but an enormous number of possible positions.
Reversi and Othello involve flipping opposing discs by trapping them between your own.
In Connect Four, the first player can force a win with perfect play.
Tic-tac-toe is a draw if both players make optimal moves.
Nim has a winning strategy based on the bitwise XOR of pile sizes.
The game of Hex cannot end in a draw if the board is completely filled.
In the game of Hex, the first player has a theoretical winning strategy on any standard board size.
A zero-sum game is one where one player's gain is balanced by another player's loss.
A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where no player benefits by changing strategy alone.
The prisoner's dilemma shows how individually rational choices can lead to a worse joint result.
Rock–paper–scissors has no winning deterministic strategy against a perfectly random opponent.
The minimax algorithm chooses moves assuming an adversary responds optimally.
Alpha–beta pruning can skip branches of a game tree without changing the minimax result.
Monte Carlo tree search balances exploring new moves with exploiting promising ones.
A game tree can grow exponentially with the number of moves searched.
In a fair coin-flipping game, losing five times does not make a win more likely on the sixth flip.
The gambler's ruin problem models how a player can go broke despite playing repeated random games.
A 20-sided die is an icosahedron, one of the five Platonic solids.
A fair d20 has a five-percent chance of rolling any particular face.
The original Dungeons & Dragons tabletop role-playing game was first published in 1974.
Magic: The Gathering was first released in 1993 and helped establish the collectible card game genre.
Spells and most abilities on Magic's stack resolve in last-in, first-out order.
In Magic, summoning sickness stops a newly controlled creature from attacking unless it has haste.
The Commander format of Magic normally uses a 100-card singleton deck including its commander.
Most Commander games in Magic begin at 40 life per player, rather than the usual 20.
Magic: The Gathering has tens of thousands of distinct cards across its history, but a normal constructed deck starts with at least 60.
The first commercial video game arcade hit, Pong, was released by Atari in 1972.
Space Invaders launched in Japan in 1978 and helped popularize arcade video games.
Alexey Pajitnov created Tetris in 1984 on the Soviet Electronika 60 computer.
The seven Tetris shapes are called tetrominoes: each is made from four unit squares.
Pac-Man was released in Japan in 1980 under the original name Puck Man.
The 1983 video game crash reshaped the North American home console market.
The NES launched in Japan in 1983 as the Family Computer, or Famicom.
The Nintendo Game Boy launched in 1989 with a monochrome LCD display.
Minecraft worlds use procedural generation instead of being designed block by block by hand.
A roguelike traditionally features procedural levels and permadeath, though definitions vary.
Speedrunners may use glitches to finish games faster than intended by their designers.
In many games, a 'seed' allows the same pseudorandom world to be regenerated.
A deterministic game simulation produces the same output from the same initial state and inputs.
The Elo rating system was originally devised for rating chess players.
Post-it Notes grew from Spencer Silver's unusual reusable adhesive and Art Fry's idea for bookmarks.
The microwave oven was inspired by Percy Spencer noticing that microwaves melted candy in his pocket.
Velcro was inspired by burrs clinging to clothing and dog fur after a walk.
The safety pin was patented by Walter Hunt in 1849 after he bent a wire into a clasp.
The first practical telephone patent was granted to Alexander Graham Bell in 1876.
Alexander Fleming noticed penicillin's antibacterial effect in a contaminated culture in 1928.
Penicillin became widely useful only after later work turned Fleming's observation into a medicine.
Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895 while experimenting with cathode rays.
Röntgen took a famous early X-ray image of his wife's hand, showing her wedding ring.
The first successful powered, controlled airplane flight by the Wright brothers lasted 12 seconds in 1903.
The Wright brothers were bicycle makers before becoming aviation pioneers.
The first traffic light was installed in London in 1868 and used gas lamps.
Electric traffic signals appeared in the early twentieth century.
The zipper emerged from several inventions before the modern interlocking design was perfected.
An early zipper-like fastener was patented by Whitcomb Judson in 1893.
The first barcode scan of a retail product used a pack of Wrigley's chewing gum in 1974.
The barcode system drew inspiration from Morse code, using patterns of lines rather than dots and dashes.
The QR code was created in 1994 by Denso Wave to track automotive parts.
QR codes include error correction so they can sometimes be read despite damage.
The lithium-ion battery was commercialized by Sony in 1991 after decades of battery research.
The first electric battery, Volta's pile, was invented around 1800.
The first incandescent lamps predated Edison; his team helped make them commercially practical.
The first practical transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in December 1947.
The first integrated circuit prototypes were developed in the late 1950s by Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce.
The laser was first demonstrated by Theodore Maiman in 1960.
The first working liquid-crystal display was demonstrated in the 1960s.
Early computer touchscreens existed decades before modern smartphones.
The first commercially successful photocopier from Xerox appeared in 1959.
Chester Carlson invented xerography before Xerox became a household name.
The first successful polaroid instant camera went on sale in 1948.
Edwin Land's instant photography system developed a photograph inside the camera.
The phonograph invented by Thomas Edison in 1877 could record and reproduce sound.
The first practical steam engines were used to pump water out of mines.
James Watt did not invent the steam engine; he greatly improved its efficiency.
The mechanical clock transformed timekeeping in medieval Europe.
The printing press with movable metal type spread through Europe in the fifteenth century.
Bi Sheng developed movable type in China centuries before Gutenberg.
Gunpowder was first developed in China and later spread to other regions.
Paper was developed in ancient China, with early surviving examples predating the Common Era.
The compass was used in China long before it became a standard navigation tool in Europe.
On 26 April 1956, the Ideal X sailed with 58 containers; container shipping expanded internationally in the 1960s.
The shipping container's standardized dimensions enable transfers between ships, trains and trucks.
An early Sputnik tracking network used radio signals from the satellite to follow its orbit.
The bicycle's modern diamond-frame form became common in the late nineteenth century.
The first pneumatic tire patent was granted to Robert William Thomson in 1845.
The world's first functioning photograph from a camera was made by Nicéphore Niépce in the 1820s.
The first modern air conditioner was designed by Willis Carrier in 1902 to control humidity.
The stethoscope was invented by René Laennec in 1816, initially using a rolled paper tube.
The first parking meters were installed in Oklahoma City in 1935 after Carl Magee developed the idea.
The first plastic LEGO brick using the modern stud-and-tube coupling was patented in 1958.
The deepest known point in Earth's oceans, Challenger Deep, lies almost 11 kilometres below sea level.
Mount Everest is Earth's highest peak above sea level, but not the farthest point from its centre.
The summit of Chimborazo is farther from Earth's centre than Everest because Earth bulges at the equator.
Mauna Kea is taller than Everest when measured from its base on the ocean floor.
Earth is an oblate spheroid, slightly flattened at the poles and wider at the equator.
Earth's equatorial diameter is roughly 43 kilometres greater than its polar diameter.
Tectonic plates move at rates comparable to fingernail growth, usually centimetres per year.
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is an underwater mountain system where tectonic plates move apart.
Most of Earth's volcanic activity occurs under the oceans rather than on land.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is home to many active volcanoes and frequent earthquakes.
Earthquakes release energy that travels through Earth as seismic waves.
S-waves cannot pass through liquids, helping scientists infer Earth's liquid outer core.
Earth has a solid inner core surrounded by a liquid outer core made mostly of iron and nickel.
Earth's magnetic field is generated largely by motion in its electrically conducting outer core.
The magnetic north pole moves over time rather than staying in one fixed spot.
Auroras occur when charged particles interact with gases high in Earth's atmosphere.
The Sahara is the largest hot desert, but Antarctica is larger if all deserts are counted.
Antarctica is classified as a desert because it receives very little precipitation.
Antarctica stores most of Earth's fresh water in its enormous ice sheet.
The Greenland ice sheet is the second-largest body of ice on Earth after Antarctica's.
The Dead Sea's surface is one of the lowest exposed land elevations on Earth.
The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system and is visible from space in satellite images.
The Amazon River carries more water than any other river on Earth by discharge.
The Nile and Amazon compete for the title of longest river because measurements vary.
Lake Baikal is the deepest freshwater lake in the world, reaching about 1,642 metres.
Lake Baikal holds about one-fifth of Earth's unfrozen surface fresh water.
The Great Lakes contain roughly one-fifth of the world's surface fresh water.
A glacier flows downhill under its own weight, even when it looks motionless.
Ice cores preserve ancient air bubbles that reveal past atmospheric composition.
The oldest known continental crust contains rocks more than four billion years old.
Zircon crystals from Western Australia are more than 4.3 billion years old.
The oldest known rocks on Earth are younger than Earth itself, which formed about 4.54 billion years ago.
The Moon's gravitational pull is a major cause of Earth's ocean tides.
The ocean's deepest trenches form mainly where one tectonic plate sinks beneath another.
Hydrothermal vents release hot mineral-rich water from the seafloor.
Deep-sea organisms around some vents depend on chemical energy rather than sunlight.
An atmospheric river is a long, narrow band carrying large amounts of water vapor.
Hailstones grow in storm clouds as rising air carries them through supercooled water.
A tornado is a rotating column of air connecting a thunderstorm to the ground.
Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are regional names for the same kind of tropical storm.
A hurricane's eye can be relatively calm even when destructive winds surround it.
The jet stream is a narrow band of strong winds high in Earth's atmosphere.
At sea level, atmospheric pressure is roughly equivalent to the pressure of 10 metres of water.
The troposphere contains most of Earth's weather and much of its atmospheric mass.
A rain shadow forms when mountains force moist air to rise, leaving drier air on the far side.
The Atacama Desert is one of Earth's driest non-polar deserts.
Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is the world's largest salt flat.
The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland formed as basalt lava cooled and cracked into columns.
The Grand Canyon exposes rock layers recording nearly two billion years of geological history.
The Himalayas formed largely from the collision of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.
